utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Good afternoon to everybody. The witness should be brought in, please. Mr. Tolimir, I just recognised you, that you had some problems sitting down. If there is any health problem, please indicate immediately if you need some assistance.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. It's a different chair, and I didn't expect the back to be where it was. But otherwise there's nothing -- no problem with me. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I'm happy about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Please sit down. Good afternoon, sir. I realise your chair is a little bit different than the chair last week. If you need some assistance to --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It's a bit low.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Yes. The court usher will assist you. Now we can see you much better. Thank you very much, and especially thank you, Mr. Thayer, for your assistance again. I think all the chairs in this courtroom have been changed over the weekend. So there is no need for further assistance for the witness. The usher should sit down, please. No, no, it's fine now, it's fine now. Come. So finally everything is arranged. May I remind you, Mr. Kingori, that the affirmation to tell the truth still applies, and Mr. Tolimir has some more questions for you. Mr. Tolimir, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Peace onto this house. I wish to greet everyone present in the courtroom, and the witness, and may the final outcome in this trial reflect God's will. Can we call up D67. This was the last document we were looking at before we adjourned. Thank you. Thank you. We can see the document now. It will shortly appear in English, I suppose. Cross-examination by Mr. Tolimir (Continued):

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This is a document sent by the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, their army's General Staff. It was signed by Rasim Delic, and this is something that we will see. And this was sent through the Command of the 1st Corps to President Izetbegovic, wherein the president is informed of the steps taken and the men taken to Srebrenica. You see, in the second paragraph, it states: "Specifically, the following has been done for Srebrenica and Zepa:" You will see there for yourself, but you can see it says: "Seventeen helicopter flights were carried out ..." And then we will have a look at the other pages. We will see who signed the document and the amount of weapons they were sent. You see what they received. Zepa is in the first column, Srebrenica in the second, and the third column stands for sum total. You see that there's heavy weaponry there, such as rocket-launchers, hand-grenades, mortars, et cetera. And you'll see it on the next page.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: Not hand-grenades but shells, artillery shells.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we turn to page 3 in order for the witness to see that the document was sent by the general of the army, Rasim Delic, to President Izetbegovic. Thank you. Can we see the last page. There you see it, "Commander, Army General Rasim Delic."

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you now answer my question? Did you know that the Muslims in Srebrenica and Zepa were getting armed and that they received their weapons by helicopter, as stated in this letter that Delic sent to the president on the 13th of July?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: And the interpreter didn't catch the year Mr. Tolimir said.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Maybe I can request you bring the first page so that I can see the date again, please.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Now we have the first page on the screen. And you should activate your microphone, Mr. Tolimir, if you have a question.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, you can see it was sent on the 13th of July, and it was forwarded through the Command of the 1st Corps to President Alija Izetbegovic. Can you tell us now, were the observers aware of the fact that arming was taking place of the enclaves of Srebrenica and Zepa by helicopter?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm not privy to the information that is in this letter because I've not seen it before, but the first time that we heard about arming of the Muslims by helicopter was through a meeting we had with Colonel Vukovic, who told us that there has been a helicopter which has been shot resupplying arms to Srebrenica. We could not confirm that, as in my report. We later on found that the chief of staff was injured. So at least we knew there was something like that, but we never saw any weapons being resupplied. We never witnessed any helicopter coming into the enclave to bring arms.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you explain how it was possible for such an amount of weapons as stated here should be sent, shipped to the enclave without the observers having any knowledge of its taking place? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, it is possible for anything to happen like this because, firstly, the armament you're talking about is not that heavy, the weaponry. In fact, there's only, I think, one rocket-launcher and, I think, one artillery piece that I have seen, so the others are small arms and ammunition. So it is possible for it to be transported there with us -- without us knowing. Secondly, being three military observers, it was very difficult to cover the whole enclave at one time, so maybe the time they are resupplying is when we are in another location. But we never saw these weapons, we never saw them having changed -- you know, the way you meet people who have re-armed themselves, changing even in the way they discussed issues with you, forcefully and stuff like that, we never noted that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Can we have the second page on the screen again. Please carry on, Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you see that it includes 16 launchers under 7, that there are 97 -- 98 pieces of RPG, 106 rifles, et cetera? And I was reading the figures for Zepa only. And Srebrenica was shipped even higher amounts; 292 RPGs, 44 launchers, et cetera. I didn't ask you to analyse the type of weapons involved here. I only wanted you to tell me how it was possible for the observers not to be aware of supplies of weapons being sent by helicopter since the territory where these helicopters landed was under the control of UNPROFOR. And these were no birds, mind you.

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I've already answered that, in that we could not be able to cover the whole enclave, and we did not notice it. We never came to know about it, other than when we were told by Colonel Vukovic about one helicopter that had crashed. We have no -- we did not have any further information, and I gave the reasons.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now turn to page 1 of D67. We will look at the fourth bullet point - that's page 2 - where General Delic reports -- it's page 2 in English, the fourth bullet point: "In preparations for a future operation to link up the enclaves, we brought in and took back four brigade commanders, two brigade chiefs of staff, and the 26th Division chief of staff. The division commander, who was meant to go on the next helicopter flight, did not return. After the final flight ended tragically, Naser remained."

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This is my question: Can you see here that General Delic was informing Alija Izetbegovic of their intention to link up the enclaves of Srebrenica and Zepa? Is that something that can be clearly seen in this document, as well as the fact that the commanders were sent to Tuzla to prepare for this operation? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: This obviously has almost the same answer, in that at these meetings of theirs, these letters that they were passing from one headquarter to another, we were unable to get them. Secondly, about the flights, we did not get to know whether they occurred. We did not see them. So I don't have any other answer.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Please look at D53 now. Can we call it up in e-court, D53. It's an order issued by the Main Staff of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: And the interpreter didn't catch the date. It was too fast.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It says "Preparation for offensive activities, orders for the Command of the 28th Division." Can the text be enlarged, please. It is stated therein: "Pursuant to a verbal order issued by the commander of the General Staff of the BH Army --" so this was a verbal order given while they were down there -- "and on the occasion of the great success achieved by units of the BH Army in the wide area around Sarajevo and Gorazde, as well as on the basis of intelligence, that the command of the army forces of the Protection Regiment in Han Pijesak is holding part of its units in reserve to intervene in the event of an attack by our forces from Zepa. I hereby issue the following order:" Under 1: "Execute all preparations in the Command of the 28th Land Army Division to execute offensive combat operations, with a view to liberating the territory of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, over-extending and inflicting losses on the aggressor forces whilst co-ordinating action with the BH Army forces carrying out operations in the broader Sarajevo area. "2. Plan realistic tasks which will assure certain success ..." And: "3. The General Staff of the BH Army will regulate, by an order, the commencement of offensive combat activities in the zone of responsibility of the 28th Army Division."

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Based on this order sent by the General Command of the BH Army on the 17th of June to the 28th Division, can you tell us, is it not true that, with this document, they were called upon to carry out offensive combat activities out of a demilitarised zone?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, the letter is self-explanatory on the same, but also --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. But you, as an observer, were you aware of the fact that offensive activities were being prepared which were to take place out of a demilitarised zone in the months of June and July, pursuant to an order from the General Staff of the BH Army?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, if you look on the screen, you see your question took a very, very long time. Then the witness tried to answer your question, and after one line and one word you interrupted him, and again you put a question to the witness. I think it would be more fair if you would let him answer as -- in that way he wants to answer. Mr. Thayer, did you want to add something? Thank you. Mr. Kingori, would you please continue with your answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, what I was saying is that the letter, itself, is self-explanatory, but we need to go deeper into this than just what we are seeing, in that the same way the Muslims, according to my own assessment, were preparing themselves, the BSA must also have been doing the same. And also we need to consider that the preparations by the Muslim side is from a point of weakness, a point whereby they are not strong enough. In fact, I don't see them having been in a position to cause any -- to start any attack on the BSA because they could not sustain it. They were not armed. The kind of arms that they had, mainly small arms, the ones that we are seeing in the least here for resupply -- for supply to that place, there are very few heavy weapons, and you can see that. The RPGs are not heavy weapons. The ones we are mentioning, 98 of them, they are not heavy weapons. Those are hand-held. So if you can look at the whole scenario, the kind of re-arming that the Muslims were having is minimal and is more mainly -- according to me, more mainly on the defensive side than offensive. I don't see them being in a position, even at that particular moment, to attack the BSA.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Let's now have a look at document P986. It's an operative report dated the 30th of June, 1995, which was sent by Mr. Becirovic to the Command of the 2nd Corps, where he reports on the combat activities taken out of the enclaves of Srebrenica and Zepa.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, kindly have a look at this document and see the number of Serb soldiers who were reported to be killed in this operation out of the demilitarised zone. You will see that in this first bullet point, below the first paragraph, it says: "Thirteen Chetniks killed. "Two light machine-guns captured. "Several dozen Chetniks wounded." And it says that: "Our casualties were two dead and three wounded." And then below paragraph 2, in the first bullet point, it says: "Seven Chetniks killed." Likewise, below paragraph 3, it is stated that: "Several successful sabotage activities were carried out in the territory occupied by the enemy, across some 20 to 40 kilometres deep within the territory in the areas of Han Pijesak and Vlasenica municipalities; namely, Visnjica settlement and Bajte stronghold, Crna Rijeka area, Vranj common feature," et cetera. In the first bullet point is stated: "Over 40 Chetniks are estimated to have been killed ..." Can we turn to the next page in e-court, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Your question will be a very long one again. I think you made the point --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Sorry. You made the point, reading some portions of it. It would be helpful if you now could put a question to the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me complete it. I'm reading the bullet point which says that 40 Chetniks were killed and 1 enemy soldier was taken prisoner. So this is the end of the quotation, and here is my question for the witness:

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you, as a military observer, have any knowledge of the fact that Muslim forces were carrying out these activities out of the demilitarised zones of Zepa and Srebrenica in the months of June and July, inflicting heavy losses on our forces, more than 40 dead? Did you have information to this effect? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, the only way that this information could have come to us, if it was passed through the BSA. In all the meetings that we held with them, they never mentioned anything like this. That means, you know, you still have to remember that war is done through propaganda, so all these things could have been propaganda in that you're sure, like, you're the one who's winning the war, whereas maybe you're losing. Secondly, the BSA, how come they never reported to us on anything like this? And to answer the question directly: We never got to know about this issue because nobody had reported to us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Was the VRS supposed to report to you or to the command -- your headquarters in Sarajevo? Were you informed about the UNPROFOR HQ of these events? Did you receive any information from them? Yes or no. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, we did not.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Could we now see the witness's statement, page 5, paragraph 2, line 1. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: For the record, that is Exhibit P992.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I apologise. I didn't say the number -- or, rather, the reference for the e-court. It's statement P992. This is page 4 in the English language version, page 6 in e-court, whereas in Serbian it's paragraph 2, line 1. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Page 6 in e-court, not page 4. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please take a look at your statement, where you say, in paragraph 2, sentence 1, I quote: "The situation was calm until the 6th of July at 300 hours, when the BSA started shelling the town of Srebrenica ..." That's the last paragraph on this page in English; page 4, that is. Now somebody turn to page 5. So: "The situation was calm until July 6th, at 300 hours, when the BSA started shelling Srebrenica town." These are the last three sentences on the previous page in English. Could we please show the witness page 4 in English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Please go back one page. Thank you. Now we have it on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is the fact that there were no combat activities behind this statement of yours until, as you say here, the BSA started shelling the town at 0300 hours -- was it really like that, that there was no combat activities until that point in time?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, I can confirm to you that there were no combat activities which were happening at that particular moment, other than this shelling that started at 300 hours on this day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Since it was calm until the beginning of the events at Srebrenica and Zepa on the 6th of July, which is the date you mentioned as the date the shelling started, until that period were there any contacts between UNPROFOR and the Serb side or UNPROFOR and the ABiH side, or did any observer complain of the fact that there were combat activities?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course, we have reports, you know, previously. The days earlier -- some days earlier, we had an attack through a tunnel. We also had a report from the RBiH, that is, the Muslim side, that they have been hit from the BSA side. You know, those reports were there. We were getting those reports earlier on, but it's sort of there was nothing much because -- let's say for sure in Srebrenica, and let's say the whole of the former Yugoslavia, there was not much activity. You know, small-arms fire, we were not calling that as a major military activity. But when it involved heavy shelling, that was an issue that had to be taken very seriously. So when we talk about the situation was calm at this particular moment, it doesn't mean that there is nobody was shooting -- you know, firing one round or two rounds in whichever place, but what we mean is that this is a change from the normal. This is actually heavy -- heavy shelling, and that is why we had to talk about it this way.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. You continue to say in your statement, on page 5 and page 6, that there was shelling, and you describe it and you count shells. And on transcript page 176 -- 1D176, I quote: "On this first day of shelling, we only had few casualties. Actually, there were injuries from shrapnel. Surprisingly, the number of casualties was not great." Also, on page 19185, you say: "Above all, I would like to say that it was very surprising to us that there was such heavy shelling, and yet when we went outside, we found a very small number of casualties or injured soldiers." So you say here when you go outside. Go outside from where? From where did you observe this shelling?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, the issue of from where, really, is -- to me is not a very big one, because you can count the shells from wherever you are, provided you are within -- you are around that area. And we were able to count from our PTT building the number of shells which were landing. And you can always know the difference between incoming and outgoing fire, so you could be able to count the shells which were landing on the enclave, both in Srebrenica, Potocari, and those other areas. Other areas where we could not be able to go, we were depending on the observation posts which were manned by DutchBat. The other question that you asked about why the casualties were that low, that was our observation. The casualty level was lower than anybody could have expected out of the heavy shelling that was in that place. We went outside there from our PTT building. We went out and did crater analysis and also took the injured and the dead to hospital, and we could be able to see the number of the casualties. We were in a position to know. The level of the casualties maybe was low because the people were inside their buildings, and we were also telling them, and it's somewhere in my statement, that we were requesting them to remain in their shelters in the buildings instead of coming out, because the shelling was for some time and then it stopped, and that was the time we were going out, and then we would go back to our PTT building.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I think you quoted from the transcript in the Popovic case. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is correct, Your Honour. Thank you, and I apologise for not making my reference clear enough.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said a minute ago that you were in a position to know the number of casualties. Can you tell us how many you saw in that period from the 6th until the 11th, that is, how many dead people and how many injured people, and what were the numbers mentioned in your report concerning these events? Because this is not in your statement.

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I hope, Your Honour, you're not pushing me into sort of analysing the number of people who were dead during the whole onslaught, because it's all documented, it's in the situation reports which we were sending, which are attached here, and I don't think I can be able to remember all the figures that I put.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. President. I also just wanted to note for the record that, in fact, if -- and I'm not sure if it's still on the screen, but Colonel Kingori's witness statement does go into detail in terms of the number of wounded and casualties that he dealt with. So if General Tolimir does have certain sections that he wants to call to the witness's attention, he's perfectly capable and knowledgeable of where those sections are. It's in his statement and it's in all the reports that are already part of the 92 bis with cross package, so I think the statement that it's not in the statement is just inaccurate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: For the record, the Popovic transcript is P950. Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, you said a minute ago that you cannot remember all the casualties during the massacre. Do you consider this shelling a massacre, and can you remember the number of those who died and were injured during the shelling, or not?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, to me, this was a massacre. That is my assessment. The aim was very clear from the beginning, even before the onslaught started; that they were to remove all the Muslims, and if the Muslims cannot be able to get out of the enclave themselves, they will kill all of them. That is the message that we got from Colonel Vukovic on several occasions. So the aim was very clear from the beginning, the mission was very clear. It was to wipe out the Muslims from that enclave. Of course, the way it was conducted was also not as good as you would call otherwise in that the shelling -- the heavy shelling that occurred in a particular area can show the aim of those who are attacking, because the most important thing in a war is, first of all, to bring your opponent to a negotiating table, yet -- you weaken him so he comes to the negotiating table. But at this particular moment, it was like to annihilate the enemy, clearly annihilate the enemy, clear the enemy from that area completely. And that's why I would say we were surprised by the low number of the casualties. Now, if we come to the figure of the casualties, it is somewhere in my report, but the total figure, really, I cannot -- I cannot remember it. Here, we are talking about those killed, those injured, and those displaced, because all of them were affected by the whole assault on the enclave.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Since you are giving evidence here, could you please describe at least one dead person you saw and where you conducted an on-site investigation or reported about the person's name? Because you speak here about genocide, about planned genocide, and I understand you, but you're not a Prosecutor; you're a witness. The Prosecutor can speak in an aggregate manner about all -- everything I'm charged with, but I would like to ask you what exactly you saw. Can you tell us?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, even in my statement, in our reports, it's indicated somewhere - I think it was the first or second day - that we picked one dead person from Srebrenica town and one injured, and we took to hospital. The others, later on after that, we have quoted the figures. But at least -- you know, you ask for one person, if I saw one, and I'm telling you I did. And not just one; I saw several. Also, in my statement, where we had -- when in Potocari, where I tried to go to a white house where the Muslims were being taken in the evening or during the day, and then gun-shots could be heard, when I tried to enter that house, I was denied access. Later on, one person was taken there, and I saw him being taken inside there. And as I was going out because I was denied access, I heard a gun-shot. And that guy did not get out of that place. We did not see him after that. What do you think happened to that person? As far as I'm concerned, he was killed, because I stayed out there, I did not see him get out. So this is evidence that people were being shot, people were being killed. Secondly, and maybe I'm [indiscernible] badly, when you threw a shell to some people, and especially civilians who are unarmed, really, you are not sending food to them. You are sending a shell to kill them, not to spare them, because if there was any intention of helping them, it would be by sending food to them, by making shelter for them, or anything else which can be humanitarian in nature, not sending artillery shells and, later on, even bringing tanks within that particular enclave. And it's quoted in my statement that we saw tanks approaching, and that is the time we left our PTT building to go to Potocari. The last part, maybe, of my answer is that finally there was an assault of the whole enclave, that is, infantry assault, which is the last part of any war, that is mopping up, ensuring that there's nobody left in that particular war zone. So all that clearly shows what happened.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know the exact name of the person who was taken to the white house? Was that reported to you by his family? And did you see the one who fired the gun-shot? Because we are here testifying about events and not about hearsay, so please tell us something that we may be able to establish through other witnesses. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, I did not see anybody pulling the trigger. If maybe I can continue. I did not see anybody pulling the trigger because, in the first place, I was not allowed to enter that house, so -- and I did not escort that person when he was going in. Secondly, they even threatened to shoot me if I dared go inside, and so I had to leave. But when I left that particular house, and we waited outside there together with UNPROFOR guys, and he did not come out. And as well, as I said earlier, we heard a gun-shot. So that is all the evidence that I have. I did not see him. I did not know his name either.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we please see P992. That's the witness's statement. Page 7 in the Serbian, first paragraph, and in English it's page 8 in e-court, the last-but-one paragraph. This is about the events that took place on the 9th of July, 1995.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can see page 7 in Serbian, paragraph 1. And in English, it's page 8, which we can also see.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Here, you say -- however, we would like to display page 8 in e-court, not page 8 of the statement. Thank you. "The building was in range." I'm reading paragraph 1. I'm on page 7 in Serbian, and that's page 8 in e-court, the last-one-one paragraph. It says: "The building was in range. We decided to abandon it and start moving toward Potocari. Osman Suljic first tried to prevent us from leaving. We convinced him of the necessity to leave for our own safety, and then he told us that we should inform everybody of the fact that chemical weapons were used against them." My question is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, I'm not sure if we have the right paragraph on the screen. I don't see --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's the right one. It's the second-last paragraph.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: In the middle, yes. Thank you. Now your question, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Have you read this part of your statement? Yes or no, so that I can put my question. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, I've read it. You can continue.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Were chemical weapons used in Srebrenica, as far as you observers knew? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, the answer is just there, in that we said we could not confirm that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Did Mr. Suljic, whom you know, want to send out a false piece of news about the use of chemical weapons in Srebrenica, and he tried to do that through you? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's difficult to say that, in that the fact that we could not confirm it, the fact that we had not seen, doesn't mean it did not happen. It's only that we had not seen it. So it was not confirmed by us, so -- and we cannot say whether it was true or not. Maybe it's in it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you please tell us whether you checked that information to establish whether it was reliable, and did you include it in your report? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's all in our report, in the sitrep that we sent to the headquarters, and we also confirmed -- you know, say that it was not confirmed by UNMOs. Secondly, that is the time -- if you can read further, that is the time we left that PTT building for the safety of ourselves, and we headed to Potocari DutchBat compound. So that time we could not -- and the war, actually, was very intensive that time. We could not go out to confirm.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you ever hear, after the event, whether or not chemical weapons were actually used in Srebrenica? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, I later heard of something like that, that chemical weapons were used. But myself, personally, I could not confirm. I just heard.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please tell the Trial Chamber from whom you heard that and when. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, it was in the internet that I searched and found something like that, something to do with Srebrenica. If you look at the internet, you see such issues being raised there. But as I said, myself, as an UNMO, I could not confirm that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Since you attached your reports to this statement as annexes, and it says on page 11 of your statement -- could we please see it? Or, rather, we have page 11 here, and it's page 12 in Serbian, line 1 --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You say in line 1, on page 12 in Serbian, and that is page 13 in English -- page 13 in e-court, mind you, you say here: "Attached to my statement ..." Attachment number 23. Can you see it on this page in English?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please tell the Trial Chamber how the reliability of that information that you included only subsequently, when you gave your statement to the OTP, can be established.

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't understand the question. Maybe you can say it again.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. In these attachments that you gave the Trial Chamber, is there anything that you put down subsequently, after the events in Srebrenica? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Maybe you can bring that document, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. You know what you gave the Trial Chamber. But is there anything that you drafted after the events in Srebrenica and that differs from the reports that UNPROFOR has and that you submitted on the very day these reports were drafted? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, in the OTP's statement of the witness he said that he provided the attachment number 23 to the OTP, not to the Trial Chamber. This is an OTP statement. I'm not sure what you are referring to. And if you want to get an answer by the witness, you should show him this attachment so that he is aware of what you are talking about.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. He has now read which attachment I'm referring to. My question is whether this attachment differs in anything from the attachment that he submitted to his superior command on the day of the events, because I don't have that one. I cannot compare. So I'm asking whether there's a difference or not. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: And Mr. Kingori asked you to show him the document. Otherwise, he will not be able to make any distinction between different documents.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. My question was whether Mr. Kingori altered any document, not just attachment 24, but any document, whether he altered anything, added anything to it after the events in Srebrenica. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Mr. President, we now have General Tolimir making allegations that the witness has altered some attachment to his OTP witness statement, and he is not giving the witness the opportunity to even look at what he's talking about. First he's talking about attachment 23, now he's alleging that he's somehow altered attachment 24. I'd like to know, first of all, what the basis for that statement is. And he's not showing us any evidence -- any support for this allegation that anything's been altered in any way. He's just asking questions with no basis and not doing the witness the courtesy of showing him what he is talking about. The accused has had these reports for years now. He knows what they are. And if he doesn't, I will read out the ERNs to these reports so that the witness can be shown. I prefer not to have to do that. I prefer that General Tolimir conducts his cross-examination with common decency and courtesy to the witness, but I will do that, and we can put them on the ELMO and we can go through every page of these attachments to see exactly what the general alleges has been somehow altered or changed or added.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, can you apply the guidance by the Chamber and the comments of Mr. Thayer and show the witness the documents you are referring to? Otherwise, you shouldn't continue in that way.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Let me first respond to what my learned friend said. He said that General Tolimir alleged. I didn't allege anything. I put a question to the witness, and I asked him if he altered any of the attachments that he submitted to the OTP. He stated here that there was attachment 24, so I asked him if there were any amendments made to it. And I can show you the attachment. It's P980. But that was not my question. My question was whether he wrote -- or added anything to it after the events in Srebrenica. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Again, Mr. Tolimir, it would be helpful if you could show the witness the document. Then he can answer your question. He requested it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I said that in e-court it's P980, but that was not my question. My question was whether he made any subsequent annotations after the events in Srebrenica. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: No, your question is if he altered something in the document or if he amended the document, and you should show the document you were referring to. Is this the document you were talking about?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. That's the document he referred to, and I quoted him on that, and that was the foundation for my question. And I asked him if, after the events in Srebrenica, he had added anything to any of the documents, in view of the fact that he was in possession of these documents up until the point he gave his statement. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Kingori.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, if it is of -- on account of whether I altered any documents, whether the ones I had or the ones which were left there, the point is that I did not alter any document at all. I don't remember altering any at all because, in the first place, any alteration could also be seen because you'd not be using the same computer that you had, you'd not be using the same satellite communication or whatever, so it's very easy to detect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And again, Mr. President, I would like to know what the basis is for this repeated allegation that there have been alterations by this witness. General Tolimir started off referring to attachment number 23, I might note for the record, and then he couldn't keep his story straight and changed it to attachment number 24. So whether it's 23 or 24, Mr. President, I think General Tolimir owes it to this witness to tell this Trial Chamber and tell this witness what his basis is -- what his good-faith basis, as an officer of the Court, is for putting that question to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: There's only one disagreement with me, at least. There was no allegation, but a question. And, of course, there's a certain allegation or estimation of Mr. Tolimir that there could have been something added or altered. Mr. Gajic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, with your permission, if I can briefly respond to Mr. Thayer. I don't know if there was an error in interpretation. The question that was put was a simple one, and the basis for the question was the very fact that the witness had these documents. So there were no allegations made, only questions. And the basis is the fact that the witness had these documents with him; nothing else.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Is the document on the screen the attachment number 23 or 24, Mr. Tolimir?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, we have attachment number 24 on our screens. And can we re-read the page of the witness's statement referring to this attachment? That's page 12 in e-court in Serbian.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Before we do that, I would like to see the whole document. That means the next page.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: The next page in English, please. Let us also see the very end of that page. It is not on the screen. It appears that this is not a complete document, because item 8 ends in the middle of a sentence. But if this is the whole document, you should proceed and again go back to P992, the OTP -- the witness statement for the OTP. Which page was it?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Page 12, line 1. That's in Serbian. In English, it's probably page 13 in e-court. Thank you. The witness was reading it a moment ago. You see on page 12 -- can we have the appropriate page in English, page 13. Laying the foundation for my question, I read the following quotation: "Attached to my statement are five pages of information we provided (attachment number 23)." Well, I didn't, myself, refer to attachment 23, as Mr. Thayer put it. I merely quoted the witness's statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, now you are referring to attachment number 23. We saw attachment number 24, one page. Here in the statement, we see an indication attachment number 24 has two pages. We only saw one page. Now you are referring to number 23. Before you put a question related to that attachment, you should put it on the screen. We haven't seen it yet.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I'm not referring to attachment number 23, I'm merely quoting the witness's statement. If he can follow in English. Maybe it was misinterpreted: "Attached to my statement, under number 23, attachment 24." So he's referring to attachments 23 and 24. I'm not doing that, myself. I only wanted to draw your attention to the fact that attachments were made to the statements that were in the possession of the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Yes, that is clear. Everybody knows it in the courtroom. If you want to put a question related to one of these two attachments, then you should put it on the screen so that the witness can see it. That's all.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't want to put a question in reference to any of this, because we will be wasting time, losing time. I only wanted to ask the witness if he had added anything to the documents that he had in his possession up until the point he gave his statement. That was all. But I will move on to my following question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: You already received a clear answer to that. He denied that. Please carry on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Can we call up 1D287 in e-court. This is a document sent by General Krstic to the Main Staff of the VRS on the 10th of July, 1995.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We can see it on our screens. Thank you. Can you enlarge it so that the witness can read it clearly.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This is a document, dated the 10th of July, which General Krstic, as the commander of the forces deployed around Srebrenica, sent in order to report on the UNPROFOR situation in the Srebrenica enclave: "On the basis of surveillance and monitoring of the situation in the Srebrenica enclave, as well as the statements of UNPROFOR soldiers who surrendered to our forces and asked for our protection, we conclude that the Muslim Army has surrounded UNPROFOR and assumed control over it. "The Muslims seized some of UNPROFOR's combat equipment (armoured combat vehicles, heavy artillery pieces, and ammunition) and are using it in combat against our forces." Chief of Staff Major General Radislav Krstic. This is my question: Were you at any point informed by the United Nations, be it during these activities or after these activities, that Muslims had been seizing combat vehicles and combat hardware? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, there's no time that we got to know about that. And as far as I knew, nothing like that happened. Unfortunately, the opposite is true; that is, it's the BSA who seized tanks belonging to the DutchBat. So that is the armoured personnel carriers, and also the soft-skinned vehicles. It is all in my statement -- I think either in my statement or some of the situation reports it is documented that the BSA seized some APCs and also soft vehicles.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell the Trial Chamber when was it that the VRS seized what you just referred to, and was it after the green signal was given where --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Can Mr. Tolimir repeat the last part of his question, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, you were asked by the interpreters to repeat the last part of the question. They were not able to catch it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell the Trial Chamber when the hardware -- the UNPROFOR hardware was seized by the VRS, and was it after Franken had issued a green alert signal, at which point he, as he put it, entered into a war against the VRS? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: As of the dates when this occurred, I really cannot remember, but it is in the report, and that the first seizure was of two APCs which were in one of the OPs, observation posts, which were taken by the BSA, and the soldiers also taken together with them. The soldiers were later given permission to leave and joined the other -- the DutchBat in Potocari, but the tanks were not released by the BSA. That was the first instance and is recorded. The second instance was when one of the soft-skinned vehicles were coming back from Bratunac. It was seized by some of their soldiers. We later on asked Major Nikolic who these soldiers were, and they said those were not the regular soldiers who took that vehicle. So whether regular or not regular, they would belong to the BSA. So at least I know of those two instances which are recorded here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know that transcripts were reviewed here and it was cleared up that this group of soldiers had surrendered to the VRS, and that General Nicolai thanked the VRS for the fact that none of them were injured and for the fact that they were transferred first to Bratunac and then to Potocari? It was the Prosecution that showed the transcript, not I.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'd be very curious to know what the citation is for General Tolimir's allegation or his contention that General Nicolai ever testified that he thanked anybody in the VRS for taking the DutchBat soldiers into captivity. I would like to know what the citation is for that proposition if that's going to be put to this witness as something that is in evidence before this Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Mr. Thayer will remember quite well that he had admitted a notation by the assistance of General Nicolai wherein it was stated that discussions took place and that General Nicolai thanked for the fact that the soldiers were transferred to Bratunac. This happened during the testimony of General Nicolai, and I asked the witness here if he was aware of it. I didn't ask him if he had read or seen the transcripts. My question had to do with his knowledge. And Mr. Thayer will be familiar with the note - it was admitted through General Nicolai - where his assistants recounted the conversation he had with Tolimir. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Kingori, can you comment on that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have no comment on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us, was the green alert signal given before the 10th? And I'm referring to the document we have on our screens, which General Krstic sent on the 10th of July.

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, I answered such a question the other day, when I said that I was not aware of the green alert. And whether -- maybe you can explain it better to me, whether it means highest level or all that, because I'm not aware of those colours or what -- I had answered that question earlier, that I do not know about their lads.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. There's no need to re-put the question. I showed you the transcript of Mr. Franken's evidence, where he said that on the 9th, 10th, and 11th, he was waging a war with the VRS, and you read those pages and said that you had no comments. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, if you may allow me to say something on that, in that the -- the issue that you are driving at, that is, on fighting from the UNPROFOR side -- the UNPROFOR side fighting the BSA, I don't think that ever happened, if I can remember very well. The point is that it reached a point where the UNPROFOR had to defend themselves, and I agree with that, that they were being targeted -- that is, the DutchBat, they were being targeted by the BSA, and it's documented that their observation posts were being targeted by the BSA. And so, really, what option were they left with? They definitely had to fire back. They had to fight their way out of those particular endangered observation posts. The fact that maybe there were some BiH soldiers behind or whatever doesn't mean that they were fighting together with the Muslims. They were just fighting their way out of a situation whereby they were being subdued by the BSA.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. I understand. I don't want to comment on what Mr. Franken said in his evidence. He was in command of these forces, and you were an observer but still did not know that this took place. It's only now that you learned of the green alert, so I won't belabour the point. Can we now call up 1D103, please. We can see it on our screens. Please look at paragraph 1 only. This is a document calling general mobilisation in Srebrenica municipality. Under 1, it reads: "Immediately mobilise all able-bodied citizens from 16 to 60 years of age for the purpose of joining TO/Territorial Defence units, Public Security stations, Civilian Protection units, and compulsory work service." The document was signed by the president of War Presidency, Mr. Hajrudin Avdic. The question is: Did you know Mr. Hajrudin Avdic? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember there was somebody by that name, but I didn't know him very well. I can't remember him. But at least I've heard that name before.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know if Srebrenica had a wartime president or a wartime presidency? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Does it follow from this document that it was the War Presidency that signed the letter, or, rather, the president, Hajrudin Avdic, on its behalf? Do you see it here in the signature block?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a letter that I never came across, so I think your assessment could be as good as mine. I don't know who signed. I don't know on behalf of whoever. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Since you are not familiar with this: Does it not follow from the document that all the able-bodied citizens of Srebrenica from 16 to 60 years of age came under the military obligation?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, that would be a generalisation which may not be very correct, in that saying that those of the age of 16 to 60 years be recruited is just a generalisation that everybody who is 16 to 60 years was recruited. I said the other day that maybe some of them could not have made soldiers. Some of them could have been injured, some of them could have been sick, some of them could have been unable to do it, anything. So, really, saying -- you know, saying this doesn't mean that those who were of this age bracket became soldiers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Isn't it correct that the authority issuing this order imposes the obligation to become mobilised upon all of the citizens, and it is down to that authority, ultimately, to decide who will be recruited or who will not? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: We'll first hear the answer, if there's an answer, and then you'll get the floor, Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, really, on this document I have got no answer. There's nothing I can say about it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: I was just wondering if there's a date on the document. There's a stamp with a date on it, but that's the date that this document was provided by the Republika Srpska commission. But I'm just wondering if there's any date that we can have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: That would exactly be my question. I would like to have the top of the page and the bottom of the page. First, the top of the page in both languages, please. Thank you. There's nothing else than we have seen earlier. Now please go to the bottom of the page. We have to note there is no date on this document, not in the original B/C/S version, nor in the English translation. The stamp contains, as Mr. Thayer already noted, the date the 27th of May, 2004, and this is the date contained in your list of documents that you indicated to use. But this is obviously a stamp of the commission for investigating the events in and around Srebrenica that was done much later, but we don't have a date of this original document. Mr. Tolimir, you indicated before the witness appeared in the Tribunal that you would use six to seven hours for cross-examination. Now you have exceeded eight hours of cross-examination. And you indicated to be able to finish during the first session of today. We are now at the end of the first session. I would like to know: How do you want to proceed?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I have three more questions, and I want to note that the ERN number here is the Prosecution's, so it's an OTP document which they probably received from the Commission for Investigating War Crimes and was disclosed as such. It wasn't admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: The first of your --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: ... before the break.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I would try to do so. However, it has to do with the map that we spent an entire session on. So in order for us to avoid time constraints, maybe I should put this question after the break, although, if need be, I can accept your suggestion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: In the meantime, we have reached the time for the first break. We will adjourn now and resume quarter past 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I would just ask the three questions that I still owe you. I owe them to you, the witness, and the Prosecution. And I must point out and draw your attention to page 1195 of the transcript of the 15th of April. It's about Mr. Groenewegen [Realtime transcript read in error "Baronjik"]. I will quote what I said to him then, because the Prosecutor asked me to quote: "Mr. Groenewegen [Realtime transcript read in error "Kingori"], you have just told us that you saw a UN truck full of refugees. Can you tell us what happened on that day when you saw the truck? Thank you." That was my question. And his answer was: "It must have been on the 10th of July." I thanked him and asked him whether the VRS was deployed at Potocari at the time. He said that he hadn't seen them then, but that is on the 10th. I still owe this to you because I made a reference to that transcript. And I have no question concerning this because it is self-explanatory that the Muslims came on the 10th of July. And this witness also said that General Mladic made an ultimatum to Mr. Karremans to the effect that he wouldn't --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: We didn't understand Mr. Tolimir's last sentence or so. Could you please repeat and rephrase.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, the interpreters asked you to repeat the last question or the last part of your last sentence. And I would like to ask you: It is not clear for me which part of your statement was a quotation and which was related to what. I really don't understand. And in page 37, line 3, I see in the transcript a quote: "Mr. Kingori, you just told us that you saw a UN truck full of refugees." Were you really using the name "Mr. Kingori"? I think there could be a mistake. Mr. Gajic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, there must have been a mistake in the translation. It's about Mr. Groenewegen and not Mr. Kingori.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: And there is another name which is unclear to me at the beginning. "Mr. Baronjik" on page 37, line 1. Whom were you referring to, Mr. Tolimir? Was it also Mr. Groenewegen?

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that's the very person.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Okay. But now, Mr. Tolimir, what is the question for this witness?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I thought of not asking any questions, because I still owed this information to the Prosecutor. But I can ask the witness a question, whether he remembers that on the 10th of July there were still Muslim refugees at the Potocari camp.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yeah, there were some.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was that why General Mladic issued one of his ultimatums to Mr. Karremans regarding these refugees at the Potocari camp?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Last time you spoke about an ultimatum, but perhaps you don't remember. But tell us, did the VRS bring those refugees on the 10th of July or was it the UNPROFOR who did it, and was any VR -- were any VRS troops at Potocari at that time?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's very clear, what I answered before, that no UNPROFORs involved in bringing the Muslims to Potocari, and I didn't see any other vehicles being used to ferry, either by the BiH or even UNPROFOR, to transport the refugees or IDPs to Potocari. I've said that before.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I have no more questions about this, but I would like to move on to another topic and I would like to show the witness a map. Could we please see document D182. That's the cessation of activities on the establishment of the UN observation post at the village of Lozina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Could you please repeat the number? It can't be D182.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. It's actually D82. I misspoke.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. We now see the document on our screens. The witness wanted to see where the village of Lozina is, so I brought a map and marked the position of that village with a label. So the village is above the blue label on the map. Could the usher kindly hand the witness the map, which is in the possession of my legal assistant, for the witness to see the position of the village of Lozina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, to clarify, we have a report on the screen, but not a map. Did you ask for a map to be brought up on the screen?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I wanted the report to be displayed on the screen because it mentions the village of Lozina on line 3. The witness said he didn't know where the village was before he saw it on the map. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: If the witness is able to find the location on the map, the map should be put on the ELMO so we all have the opportunity to see it when the witness has found the location.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's the location, sir [indicates].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Do you have any additional question to that? I remember that you had many questions related to this location. Now you may put a question to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you now reply if you know to what this document refers, now that you've seen the location of the village of Lozina, and what this meeting between the UNPROFOR and somebody else was about concerning the cessation of activities there?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's remark: We didn't understand all the accused said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, the interpreters didn't catch all what you have said or meant.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I asked the witness whether he can answer now, having seen the location of the village of Lozina, why the activities in that village, the engineering works, stopped, the work on erecting an UNPROFOR observation post.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't think I have a proper answer to this, because in that particular area I don't remember there being a lot of activities, and so I really cannot remember the reason why they were prevented -- that is, the DutchBat were being prevented from erecting an OP there.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember or did anybody of the UN soldiers tell you that they were blocked by the Muslims, that some 100 soldiers were in that position, amongst whom were the deputy commander, Mr. Fortin? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: We need to do a couple of things here, Mr. President. The first is there's a reference to the deputy commander, Mr. Fortin, and I presume that's then Major, now Colonel Franken that is being referred to, number 1. And, number 2 -- well, I'll just leave it at that and see how the remainder of the questioning goes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Are you able to answer the question?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, sir. I can't remember the reason why they were prevented.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Kingori, you indicated the location of this village, Lozina. I can't see it very properly on the map, but it looks like "Letnja" [phoen] and not "Lozina."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's the one that is highlighted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Yes, it's highlighted.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Maybe it's the pronunciation. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: But I see "Letnja," L-e-t-n-j-a.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It's true, that's what I can see also, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Or L-o-z-n-j-a. It's an O, yes. But is that the same as the village we were discussing earlier? That was Lozina. I think there's a difference. Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: I think -- without testifying, I think I can represent the Prosecution's position that Loznja and Lozina are in fact the same villages, as far as the Prosecution is concerned. There's no dispute that we're talking about the same villages, the one that's identified here on the map and the one that's identified in the exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: That's also the position of the Defence?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. That is the position of the Defence as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In this document, in the third line from the top, the village of Lozina is spelled with a double Z, which stands for the letter "zez" with a diacritic, which isn't in the English alphabet. The English alphabet doesn't have it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Now I think it's clear, for the record, the village to which we're referring. Your next question, Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My following question is: Did the UN observers attend the meeting about this problem that had come about in the village of Loznja?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, for this particular meeting, you can see we had been represented by Romilton of Brazil.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. In the fourth paragraph, that is the fourth line, it says that the meeting was attended by the chief of the military observers, Romilton from Brazil, and that he supported the Muslim proposal that the works involved in the erection of the observation post be halted. My question is whether he spoke about the problems in that village of Loznja.

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, he did not discuss it. In fact, I really do not remember anyone telling me about the problem in that particular area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I think the map can be removed from the ELMO, if there's no need to use it any further. Then it may be given back to the Defence. It is not possible to -- it is not possible to receive it as a document or to mark it for identification because it is not in e-court. Carry on, Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Since Mr. Romilton, as the chief of the observers, supported the removal of the UN observation post from that location, can you tell us whether the principle of pencil and note-book was substituted by the gun-and-bullet approach, as far as the UN observers are concerned?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, I really do not understand what you are after here in that question. Really, I can't get a glimpse of what you are talking about. So, please, can you -- I request you frame it again in a better way, in an easier way.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Have you heard that the chief of the observers, Romilton, supported the Muslims and requested that the UNPROFOR remove the observation post? Yes or no. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't think this is a question of yes or no, because the way I answered the other day is that really I cannot remember the reasons why it was to be removed. And even now I've already said that I cannot remember the reason why it was being removed, and so I cannot be able to elaborate any further.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell me why UNPROFOR has a different attitude, because they want to erect an observation post to see what's happening on the ground, and the observers, whose attitude is opposed, and obviously don't want anybody to see what's going on on the ground?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't think that was the situation on the ground at that particular time. I said I cannot remember what happened, but on the account that you're saying that military observers actually were supporting it and that the UNPROFOR was not supporting it, I don't think that was the main thing. The main thing is, when you go for a meeting, you agree. Sometimes you may not necessarily have to all agree, but what came out of that meeting is that it should not be erected there. So it really does not matter who was opposing or who was not opposing. You know, it's a matter of them agreeing finally. You don't have to have the same feelings about the same thing. So what came out is what is more important than the discussions that they had, whoever supported, you know, whoever did not support. Provided they agreed on the same thing, that is okay.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. I would like to finish off this problem with the following question: Did you know that this village and its wider surroundings were a corridor between the enclaves of Srebrenica and Zepa, and that this was a reason for separating the two enclaves forcefully with weapons? Were you familiar with that or not?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, almost everywhere in the enclave, and especially to the southern and south-western side, was a way through to Zepa, almost everywhere there. And obviously the BSA should be able to tell us better about it because they were the ones negotiating with the Muslims on how to go and how to come back. So that's the answer I can give.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. You're answering to the Trial Chamber, and they will assess the value of your answers. I don't need them. My question to you is: Document D67, paragraph 4, when Delic said -- that's the one we read earlier.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could Mr. Tolimir please read slowly because we cannot follow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, I have to stop you because the interpreters couldn't catch that. It was too fast again, and we don't know which document you are using while reading. Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Mr. President, Colonel Kingori has been here for a while. He's a grown man, he's a military officer. He can handle himself. But if General Tolimir truly believes, as he just said, that he doesn't need the witness's answers, then he should stop asking questions, or, in the alternative, treat this witness with a modicum of respect that is befitting this Tribunal and befitting this witness's stature as one of the only heros who was on the ground in Potocari during those days when that population was removed. I would ask that General Tolimir extend that simple decent courtesy to this witness or stop his questioning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I must confess, Mr. Tolimir, I was astonished about your comment as well. You requested the witness to answer to the Trial Chamber, you don't need the answers. I don't know why you are stating that. You indicated before the break you have three additional questions. You have now put more questions to the witness. It's again half an hour of cross-examination. You should now put the last question to the witness. You should now put the last question to the witness, and I hope you will be able to finish.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. In no way did I offend this witness throughout my examination. What I meant to say was that the Trial Chamber would be assessing the witness's evidence, and not I. I never asked him to give the sort of questions [as interpreted] that would be in my favour. I'm merely asking him to answer them. And the question I was about to put had to do with D67, which we have before us now, and let's look at the fourth bullet point. That's page 2 in English. The second bullet point in English and the fourth in Serbian. It reads: "In preparations for a future operation to link up the enclaves, we brought in and took back four brigade commanders, two brigade chiefs of staff, and the 28th Division chief of staff. The division commander, who was meant to go on the next helicopter flight, did not return. After the final flight ended tragically, Naser remained." Based on this document --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: This is the second time today that you read this portion into the transcript. What is the reason? What is the need for that? Put a question to the witness. It should be the last one.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I withdraw the question. Let's move on to my last question. May I put my last question, by your leave?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Please carry on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Can we call up P963, page 2. It's a portion of a report on Srebrenica, drafted by the Dutch Institute for War Documentation. That's section 4, chapter 5 of the report. We're interested in paragraph 3. Since there is no translation, Serbian translation, I'll read it out in Serbian and you'll have it in English on your screens. I'm quoting: "At the time --" And the reference is to the 9th of July, 1995: "At the time that the UNMOs left Srebrenica in a great hurry --" and "UNMOs" is short for "observers," that's my explanation, so I'll start again: "At that time, the UNMOs left Srebrenica in a great hurry ..." And again the reference is to the 9th of July: " ... one of them, the Dutch Major De Haan, was already at the compound in Potocari. He had arrived there on July the 1st for some minor surgery, but had hung around the compound ever since, to the annoyance of many DutchBat members. De Haan, himself, declared that he had gone back to work on July the 10th, inside the compound as well as outside it. The former was something that depended on how you looked at it. The remaining UNMOs, UN observers, Kingori and Tetteh, already joined him on July 9th, when things got too hot for them, and they left the compound again only after the fall of the enclave. They didn't make a very good impression when they sent their interpreter, Emir Suljajic, back to Srebrenica with a Motorola walkie-talkie to count and report on the shell bursts. Some DutchBat soldiers liked to call the UNMOs 'UNBOs,' standing for 'UN Bunker Observers,' because 'when something had to be observed, these people were sitting in the bunkers.' Two interpreters also said later that the United Nations Military Observers hardly ever tried to set foot outside the door and very much relied on them." The interpreters, in other words. "Lieutenant-Colonel Karremans also made a vain attempt to send them back to Srebrenica. 'When that failed, I sent my own liaison officer team.'"
